name: Femi Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit library shelves and timber counters at the Stone Road learning centre. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and experienced enough to set out a normal room, though I still ask the lead when a wall hides a pipe. My partner Clara works in a hospital laundry, and our grown sons live on their own. The builder pays the usual rate, we have about four months of expenses saved and some other carpentry firms nearby. I use an AI tool now and then to clarify a catalogue code, then compare the answer with the printed order before cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small software saving is welcome if it means fewer wrong brackets for the shelves. We still have to find the studs and make a counter fit the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my wage and Clara's hospital hours to continue in this mild picture. Four months saved is not endless, but it covers a normal pause and there are other builders I could ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting shelves and check catalogue codes against the printed order. In the first year I'd continue the usual savings transfer and ask lead carpenter Dina when the next library room becomes available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about a modest change. The tougher part of my week is an old wall with no stud where the drawing says there should be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the catalogue tool made a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once found a bracket with the right name but the wrong load rating, which Dina caught on the paper sheet. I use the phone tool for finding a catalogue code, not deciding what can hold a full shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about the next room already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to plan the crew's time and not lose a paid morning waiting for the room to clear. I ask about that even when nobody mentions AI.

say: I'd welcome **fewer wrong brackets** from checked catalogue searches.
I'd remind the crew **shelves still need studs** and careful fitting.
think: My wage and Clara's **hospital hours** look steady.
Our **four-month reserve** and nearby builders cover an ordinary pause.
do: Keep fitting **library shelves** and checking catalogue codes.
Continue the **usual savings transfer** and ask Dina for room dates.
feel: **Settled** about small software changes, focused on old-wall surprises.
S0.quote: I use the phone tool for finding a catalogue code, not deciding what can hold a full shelf.
fieldNote: Femi's occasional AI use is limited by a **wrong load rating** caught on paper.
Typical pay, Clara's regular work and a **four-month reserve** support a calm mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep fitting paid shelves at the Stone Road centre
Use AI for catalogue codes after checking printed load ratings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying software may speed up orders, but workers should see how wrong parts get corrected. I would ask the union steward for paid time to test a shelf order beside the buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could do estimates with fewer people, and that may make the next site less certain. I am still needed to find studs and fit shelves, so my own pay seems reasonably safe for now, but I want the contract dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare a live software order with the brackets and boards that arrive, then keep taking centre shifts. If the next contract is delayed, I'll check two local builders for paid work and ask the steward to record any hours the crew loses fixing order errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about the tool and uneasy for the office staff. My household can cover a short delay, but it should not be hidden inside a claim that the new system saves money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bracket with the wrong load rating could put books and people at risk. I'd want the buyer and fitter to sign off the same specification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the buying screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a couple of real orders arrived correctly, yes, on paid time. I pick up tools when someone has shown they work for our job.

say: I'd ask for **paid order testing** with the buyer.
I'd require a clear route to correct **wrong shelf parts**.
think: Fewer office staff may make the **next site uncertain**.
My hands-on fitting and **four-month cushion** protect my immediate income.
do: Compare a **live shelf order** with delivered parts.
Keep **centre shifts** and check local builders after a delay.
Report **lost correction hours** to the union steward.
feel: **Curious and uneasy**, with concern for office colleagues and hidden costs.
S1.quote: A bracket with the wrong load rating could put books and people at risk.
fieldNote: Femi's first test concerns a **load-rated bracket**, connecting software accuracy to public safety.
He expects current site pay to hold while asking the union to count **hidden correction hours**.

steps.text: Learn the buying screen after two successful paid shelf orders
Check two local builders if the next contract is delayed
Report lost correction hours to the union steward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch thinking AI in 2028 may alter estimates and orders, while robots able to fit shelves arrive around 2031. I would ask for a worker seat at a safe site trial before the builder changes the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when office work changes and sixty-three when robots could set the counters and shelves. Four months saved gives Clara and me a little search time, but her hospital wage alone may not cover rent if I lose my site income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask the union for written notice of robot trials and check the digital load-rating tool with Dina. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid shelf work while available, and if the roster shrinks I'll apply to the two local renovation teams before spending down the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a meaningful wage by sixty-three. I can still compare tools and approach employers, but our savings are too small to call the change harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real loaded shelf, a stop switch workers can reach and a named person who signs off the fixing. A showroom shelf with no books on it would not answer me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for another trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd consider a funded paid placement if a real local employer offered one. I would not leave four months of savings to carry an unpaid course.

say: I'd separate **2028 office tasks** from 2031 hands-on shelving robots.
I'd ask for a **worker seat** at robot trials.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot fitting could take my site wage.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot replace that income for long.
do: Request **written robot notice** and check load-rating software.
Apply to **renovation teams** if the roster shrinks.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss, with time for applications and checks.
S2.quote: A showroom shelf with no books on it would not answer me.
fieldNote: Femi locates income risk at the **2031 robot date**, after office estimates change.
He requires a **loaded real shelf** and reachable stop switch before treating a site robot as safe.

steps.text: Ask the union for written notice of robot trials
Check the digital load-rating tool with Dina
Keep taking paid shelf shifts in 2029
Apply to two renovation teams if the site roster shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to collect proper test results and agree who checks machine-fitted shelves. I would ask the branch for yearly staffing and safety reports, not a one-day demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots may do the site fitting. Clara and I might want fewer workdays by then, but we cannot know whether our income and savings will cover it without actual figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid shelf and counter jobs and ask the steward for annual safety results. In 2032 I'd take fitting shifts if offered, use the proven catalogue tool for codes and sit with Clara to compare our savings with bills; if site bookings vanish, I'd apply to nearby builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed by the longer warning, though I still want evidence rather than a sales talk. Time is useful if we keep earning through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide whether you work fewer days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our rent, health costs, Clara's wages and what we really have saved. I will not tell our sons a retirement date until the household figures add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train to inspect the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there were a paid local role and proper safety instruction, I'd consider it. I wouldn't enrol in a course just because a manager says inspectors will be needed.

say: I'd seek **yearly safety reports** before machine-fitted shelves spread.
I'd demand a **named checker** for every installed shelf.
think: At **sixty-six**, fewer workdays depend on actual household figures.
I cannot assume **retirement income** will cover rent and health costs.
do: Keep **paid fitting work** and request annual safety reports.
Review **bills with Clara** and apply elsewhere if site work vanishes.
feel: Less **pressed**, but still asking for real evidence and wages.
S3.quote: I will not tell our sons a retirement date until the household figures add up.
fieldNote: Femi turns the longer period into **annual safety evidence** and household budgeting.
He considers inspection training only with a **paid local role**, without claiming to have enrolled.

steps.text: Request annual shelf-robot safety reports through the union steward
Keep taking paid fitting shifts in 2032
Use the proven catalogue tool for checked part codes
Apply to nearby builders if site bookings vanish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives workers time to learn what machines can really do and set safety rules around them. I would still teach apprentices to find a stud with their own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can fit shelves. I may be retired by then, or I may still need paid light repairs; Clara and I have not seen the future numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid carpentry while fit and put money aside after full months. In 2037 I'd accept lighter shelf repairs if we still need income, ask the union how AI-written orders are checked and review our actual bills before leaving site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about machines arriving that far away. The next decade gives us work and time to decide, provided the site jobs stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown sons help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I'd enjoy their visits, but I will not count their pay in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Find the stud, check the bracket rating and show me the loaded shelf. A person has to trust the fixing before a child pulls on it.

say: I'd ask workers to set **robot safety rules** over the decade.
I'd teach apprentices to **find studs** before trusting software.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid light repairs might still be useful.
At **seventy-one**, retirement depends on Clara and me checking real figures.
do: Keep **paid carpentry** and save after full months.
Take **lighter shelf repairs** in 2037 if needed.
Review **AI order checks** and household bills before leaving work.
feel: **Calm** about distant machines, with time to decide if work holds.
S4.quote: A person has to trust the fixing before a child pulls on it.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** leaves room for paid work and eventual retirement without assuming either outcome.
His old-fashioned **stud check** remains central even as he uses catalogue AI occasionally.

steps.text: Keep taking paid shelf-fitting shifts while fit
Save after full paid site months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most, since robots could reach my shelving work by sixty-three before Clara and I know whether we can lose my wage. Written notice, tested load checks and paid local openings would help us choose before the reserve runs down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs off a shelf after a robot puts it on an old wall. A neat photograph cannot tell a parent whether a loaded shelf will stay up.
